gloss_terse: Decay or corrosion that eats through fabric; leprous deterioration in textiles
gloss_readable: This rare Hebrew term appears only in the priestly regulations concerning leprosy in fabrics (Leviticus 13:55). It describes a destructive process—a boring or eating through of material that renders a garment ritually unclean. The word captures the consuming nature of the decay, as if something is actively devouring the fibers. The multilingual evidence (corrosion, corroding) emphasizes the penetrative, destructive aspect rather than simple surface contamination.

senses.1: Refers specifically to the leprous decay that eats through woven or knitted fabric, described in Leviticus 13:55 as part of the priestly examination of contaminated garments. The term emphasizes the penetrating, corrosive quality of the deterioration—not merely surface discoloration but active consumption of the material itself. The consistent translation as 'corroding' across European languages highlights this eating-through quality.

gloss_terse: Set free, exempt from duties; those released from regular obligations (Ketiv variant)
gloss_readable: This form appears in 1 Chronicles 9:33 in a Ketiv reading, describing Levitical singers who were exempt from other temple duties. The root meaning involves separation or removal—setting someone free from obligations. The singers were 'set apart' in a double sense: consecrated for their musical ministry, yet released from the routine work that occupied other Levites. The Spanish 'libres' (free) captures this sense of exemption well.

senses.1: Describes Levitical temple musicians who were released from other duties, found in 1 Chronicles 9:33 (Ketiv reading). These individuals were functionally 'free' or exempt because their musical ministry required full-time dedication. The term comes from a root meaning to separate or set free, and here indicates a special class status—freed from normal Levitical obligations to focus on sacred song day and night.

gloss_terse: That which opens; the firstborn as opener of the womb
gloss_readable: Used in the construct form in Numbers 8:16, this term designates the firstborn as 'opener of the womb.' It's part of the theological rationale for consecrating the Levites—they serve as substitutes for all Israel's firstborn, who belonged to God as the ones who first opened their mothers' wombs. The concept ties biological primacy (being first) to covenantal obligation. The multilingual translations preserve the opener/opening imagery, emphasizing the act of breaking through, inaugurating life.

senses.1: Refers to the firstborn as 'opener of the womb' in Numbers 8:16, where God claims every firstborn Israelite as His own because they were the first to open their mothers' wombs. This construct form emphasizes the act of opening or breaking through, connecting biological firstness with sacred obligation. The Levites are given to God as substitutes for these firstborn 'openers,' a key element in Israel's cultic system.

gloss_terse: Pi-beseth: Egyptian city sacred to the goddess Bastet, near modern Zagazig
gloss_readable: This Egyptian place name appears in Ezekiel 30:17 in a judgment oracle against Egypt. The city's name derives from Per-Bastet, 'House of Bastet,' referring to the feline goddess worshiped there. Greek sources knew it as Bubastis. Located about 30 miles northeast of Cairo (modern Tell Basta near Zagazig), it was a significant religious center. Herodotus describes its grand festival. Ezekiel prophesies that its young men will fall by the sword—Egypt's sacred places would offer no protection from divine judgment.

senses.1: An Egyptian city mentioned in Ezekiel 30:17, known in Greek as Bubastis and located near modern Zagazig. The name means 'House of Bastet,' the cat-headed goddess who was the city's patron deity. Ezekiel includes it in his prophecy of Egypt's coming destruction under Babylon, where even cities sacred to Egyptian gods would not escape judgment. The site was famous in antiquity for its temple and festivals honoring Bastet.

gloss_terse: Edges or pieces of fat from sacrificial animals; suet portions in offerings
gloss_readable: This term occurs in Judges 3:16, though BDB connects it with a different root found in Leviticus describing portions of sacrificial fat. The word refers to the pieces or edges of the fat-rich parts of sacrificial animals, particularly the suet that was burned as offerings. In the Levitical system, specific fatty portions belonged to God and were consumed on the altar. The 'edges' or pieces terminology suggests the cutting and arrangement of these choice portions during the sacrificial ritual.

senses.1: Designates the fatty portions or pieces of sacrificial animals mentioned in Levitical offerings (Judges 3:16 context, though primarily a Levitical term). These were the choice pieces of suet—the hard fat around organs—that were arranged on the altar as God's portion. The term 'edges' or 'pieces' suggests how these fatty sections were cut and separated from the meat, representing the richest parts given wholly to the Lord in burnt offerings.

gloss_terse: Superabundance of fat; excessive bodily fatness as a metaphor for complacency
gloss_readable: Appearing only in Job 15:27, this word describes excessive accumulation of fat—not the sacrificial kind, but the repulsive abundance that speaks of indulgence and moral complacency. Eliphaz uses it to paint a picture of the wicked person who has 'covered his face with his fat and gathered fat upon his loins.' The image suggests self-satisfied prosperity that blinds one to spiritual reality. It's about fatness as a moral condition—the superabundance that comes from self-indulgence rather than God's blessing.

senses.1: Describes excessive bodily fat in Job 15:27, used by Eliphaz to characterize the wicked person who has grown complacent through prosperity. The term appears in parallel with 'his fat,' emphasizing not healthy abundance but superabundance—the gross accumulation that comes from self-indulgence. The image of covering one's face with fatness suggests being blinded by material comfort, losing moral and spiritual perception in the process.

gloss_terse: Tottering, shaking; the trembling of knees in terror or weakness
gloss_readable: This vivid term appears in Nahum 2:10 (or 2:11 in some versifications) in a prophecy of Nineveh's fall. The phrase 'tottering of knees' captures the physical manifestation of terror—legs that can no longer hold steady. It's part of a cascade of images: melting hearts, knocking knees, anguish in every body, faces drained of color. The word conveys that involuntary shaking when fear grips the body so thoroughly that even basic functions like standing become difficult. Nineveh's warriors, once terrifying, would themselves become paralyzed with dread.

senses.1: Describes the trembling or tottering of knees in Nahum 2:10, part of the prophet's vivid depiction of terror overtaking Nineveh's inhabitants during the city's fall. The term captures involuntary shaking—knees that fail to support the body when extreme fear seizes a person. Used alongside images of melting hearts and pale faces, it portrays the complete physical breakdown that accompanies overwhelming dread, reducing mighty warriors to trembling invalids.

gloss_terse: Pishon: one of the four rivers flowing from Eden in Genesis 2
gloss_readable: The Pishon is named as the first of four rivers branching from the river that watered Eden (Genesis 2:11). It reportedly wound through the land of Havilah, where gold, bdellium, and onyx were found. The river's identification remains uncertain—theories have ranged from Persian Gulf waterways to African rivers to purely symbolic geography. What's clear is that it represented abundance and blessing, flowing from God's garden into lands rich with precious resources. The name itself may relate to a root meaning 'to spring forth' or 'flow,' fitting for a river bearing Eden's life-giving water to the world.

senses.1: One of the four rivers flowing from Eden in Genesis 2:11, described as winding through Havilah, a land of gold, aromatic resin, and precious stones. Though its exact location is debated, the Pishon represents the outward flow of Eden's blessing—life-giving water reaching beyond the garden to enrich distant lands. The name may derive from a root meaning 'to spring forth,' capturing the river's role as a channel of divine abundance from Paradise to the wider world.

gloss_terse: Trickling, flowing gently; water seeping or flowing out gradually
gloss_readable: This Piel participle appears in Ezekiel 47:2, describing water trickling from the south side of the temple threshold in the prophet's vision. The term emphasizes gentle, gradual flow—not a torrent but a steady seeping. This trickling becomes the river of life that grows deeper and wider as it flows east, eventually bringing healing to the Dead Sea. The choice of a word for gentle flowing (rather than gushing or pouring) heightens the miraculous nature of the vision: even a trickle from God's presence becomes a life-transforming flood.

senses.1: Describes water trickling or flowing gently from the southern threshold of the temple in Ezekiel 47:2. The Piel participle emphasizes a steady, gentle seepage rather than a powerful gush—water that begins as a mere trickle from under the temple. This modest beginning makes the vision's development more striking, as this trickling water grows into a mighty river bringing life and healing wherever it flows, transforming even the Dead Sea.

gloss_terse: The Palluites: descendants of Pallu, a clan within the tribe of Reuben
gloss_readable: This gentile adjective appears in Numbers 26:5 in the census of Israel's clans. The Palluites were descendants of Pallu, one of Reuben's four sons. As Reuben was Jacob's firstborn, these clans traced their lineage back to Israel's earliest generations. The census context emphasizes tribal identity and inheritance rights—each clan's count mattered for land distribution in Canaan. The use of the article ('the Palluites') treats them as a recognized, defined community within Israel's larger tribal structure.

senses.1: A clan designation in Numbers 26:5 for descendants of Pallu, son of Reuben. Used with the definite article ('the Palluites'), it identifies a recognized family group within Reuben's tribe during the wilderness census. This census determined not just military strength but also inheritance portions in the promised land, so clan identity carried legal and territorial significance. The Palluites represent one of the family lineages preserving Reuben's heritage as Israel's firstborn tribe.

gloss_terse: Divided, split; being partitioned or separated into parts (Aramaic)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic passive participle appears in Daniel 2:41, in Daniel's interpretation of Nebuchadnezzar's dream statue. The divided kingdom of iron and clay represents a realm that is internally fragmented—united in name but divided in nature, strong yet brittle. The term captures political and social fracture: a kingdom that cannot hold together because its constituent parts don't bond. The image of mixed iron and clay that won't adhere became a powerful metaphor for unstable empires throughout history, regimes imposing unity on fundamentally incompatible elements.

senses.1: An Aramaic passive participle in Daniel 2:41 describing the fourth kingdom in Nebuchadnezzar's dream as 'divided.' The term indicates internal fragmentation—a realm outwardly unified but inwardly split, like iron and clay that cannot truly merge. This division renders the kingdom unstable despite its strength, a powerful empire nonetheless vulnerable because it cannot achieve genuine cohesion among its disparate peoples or factions.

gloss_terse: Half, portion; one-half of a whole (Aramaic)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic noun appears in Daniel 7:25, in the phrase describing how long the little horn will persecute the saints: 'a time, times, and half a time.' The 'half' is crucial to the formula—it indicates an incomplete period, a time cut short. This broken or limited duration suggests that while persecution seems to last forever to those suffering it, God has set definite boundaries. The evil reign won't run its full course; it will be truncated. The half-time brings the sequence to an incomplete, broken end, emphasizing divine sovereignty over human oppression.

senses.1: An Aramaic word for 'half' appearing in Daniel 7:25 in the prophetic phrase 'a time, times, and half a time,' describing the duration of persecution by the little horn. This 'half' is theologically significant—it represents an incomplete period, a time cut short by divine intervention. Rather than allowing evil to run its full course, God limits it to a broken, truncated span, reassuring the faithful that their suffering has definite, divinely-set boundaries.

gloss_terse: Streams, divisions; channels of water or possibly subdivisions of a tribe
gloss_readable: This word appears in Job 20:17 with clear reference to streams of oil and honey, representing luxurious abundance the wicked will never enjoy. The same form occurs in Judges 5:15-16 where it may mean either 'streams' or 'divisions' of Reuben—the ambiguity has prompted debate about whether Deborah is criticizing Reubenites for staying by their water channels or for remaining divided into factions. The root carries both senses of flowing water and splitting/dividing, making the dual meaning natural in Hebrew. In Job's context, the 'streams' imagery is unmistakable: rivers flowing with the richest substances.

senses.1: Refers to streams or channels of liquid in Job 20:17, specifically 'streams of oil and honey'—an image of luxurious abundance that the wicked will never experience despite their temporary prosperity. The term evokes rivers flowing not with mere water but with the richest substances, representing the complete, overflowing blessing that comes from God alone. Zophar uses this imagery to contrast the fleeting pleasures of wickedness with the permanent joys reserved for the righteous.

gloss_terse: In their divisions; according to organizational sections or courses (Aramaic)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic phrase appears in Ezra 6:18, describing how the priests and Levites were set in their divisions for the service of God's house in Jerusalem. After the exile, reconstituting temple worship required organizing the clergy into their traditional courses or divisions. The term emphasizes structured, orderly worship—each group knowing its time and role. This wasn't arbitrary assignment but restoration of the Davidic system where priestly families served in rotation. The divisions ensured continuous temple service while distributing the honor and responsibility across all qualified families.

senses.1: An Aramaic phrase meaning 'in their divisions' in Ezra 6:18, describing the organizational structure of priests and Levites serving in the restored Jerusalem temple. The term indicates the traditional courses or divisions dating back to David's organization—family groups serving in rotation to maintain continuous temple worship. This structure ensured both order and equity, with each priestly family having its appointed time. Restoring these divisions was part of reconstituting authentic worship after the Babylonian disruption.

gloss_terse: Steel or iron fittings; hardened metal fixtures or ornaments on chariots
gloss_readable: This rare word appears in Nahum 2:3, describing the steel (or iron) fittings of chariots that flash like fire as Nineveh's attackers prepare for battle. The term refers to hardened metal—possibly steel, though steel technology was limited in the ancient Near East. More likely, it designates specially hardened iron or iron overlays used to reinforce war chariots or provide decorative fittings. When these metal surfaces caught the light during military maneuvers, they created flashing, fire-like effects that announced an army's terrifying approach. The word may be a loan from Persian, suggesting advanced metallurgy.

senses.1: Refers to steel or hardened iron fittings on chariots in Nahum 2:3, creating a fire-like flash during battle preparations. The term likely describes metal reinforcements or ornamental fixtures that caught and reflected light dramatically as armies maneuvered. Whether actual steel (rare in the period) or specially hardened iron, these fittings enhanced both the durability and the psychological impact of war chariots, their gleaming surfaces announcing military might as effectively as trumpets.

gloss_terse: Pildash: son of Nahor and Milcah, Abraham's nephew
gloss_readable: Pildash appears in Genesis 22:22 in the genealogy of Nahor, Abraham's brother. He was one of eight sons born to Nahor by his wife Milcah, making him Abraham's nephew. These Nahorite genealogies establish connections between Israel and the Aramean peoples of northern Mesopotamia. While Pildash himself disappears from the biblical narrative, his inclusion in this family list preserves Abraham's wider kinship network—relationships that would matter when Abraham sent his servant to find a wife for Isaac among 'his relatives,' and when Jacob fled to Laban, another descendant of Nahor.

senses.1: A personal name in Genesis 22:22, identifying one of the eight sons born to Nahor (Abraham's brother) and Milcah. As Abraham's nephew, Pildash was part of the Aramean family network centered in northern Mesopotamia. Though he plays no active role in the biblical narrative, his inclusion in this genealogy establishes the broader kinship connections between Abraham's immediate family and the related peoples of Paddan-aram, connections that become important in later marriage arrangements.

gloss_terse: Pilha: post-exilic Israelite leader who sealed Nehemiah's covenant
gloss_readable: Pilha was among the leaders who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah 10:24 (English versification), committing themselves and the people to Torah observance after the exile. This covenant-sealing ceremony followed Ezra's public reading of the Law and the people's confession of sin. Those who signed represented the community's leadership—priests, Levites, and heads of families taking corporate responsibility for Israel's faithfulness. Pilha's signature placed him among this circle of post-exilic reformers determined to avoid the mistakes that had led to exile.

senses.1: A personal name in Nehemiah 10:24, identifying one of the leaders who sealed the covenant of Torah observance in post-exilic Jerusalem. By affixing his seal, Pilha joined other heads of families in taking corporate responsibility for Israel's commitment to God's Law. This covenant represented the community's determination to rebuild not just the city's walls but its spiritual foundations, learning from the exile and dedicating themselves to faithful obedience.

gloss_terse: For the service; for the worship or cultic ministry (Aramaic)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic phrase appears in Ezra 7:19, in the Persian king's decree authorizing Ezra to take temple vessels back to Jerusalem 'for the service of the house of your God.' The term encompasses both worship and practical ministry—everything needed for temple operations. It's striking that a Persian official uses this language, recognizing that these vessels weren't just valuables but sacred implements with religious purpose. The phrase captures the functional nature of worship: service (avodah) involves both liturgical acts and the practical work of maintaining God's house and supporting its ministers.

senses.1: An Aramaic phrase meaning 'for the service of' in Ezra 7:19, referring to the cultic worship and practical ministry of the Jerusalem temple. The Persian king uses this term in authorizing the return of sacred vessels, acknowledging their religious purpose. 'Service' here encompasses both liturgical worship and the supporting work needed to maintain temple operations—a comprehensive term for everything involved in honoring God through the temple system.

gloss_terse: The Paltite: a gentile designation from Beth-pelet in Judah
gloss_readable: This gentile adjective appears in 2 Samuel 23:26, identifying Helez, one of David's mighty warriors, as 'the Paltite.' The designation links him to Beth-pelet, a town in southern Judah. David's elite fighting force drew from across Israel's tribes and regions, and these geographic identifiers preserve the warriors' origins. The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 11:27 confirms this connection. For these mighty men, their hometown designation became part of their identity—not just 'Helez' but 'Helez the Paltite,' forever associating personal valor with local roots.

senses.1: A gentile designation in 2 Samuel 23:26 identifying Helez as originating from Beth-pelet in southern Judah. As one of David's thirty mighty warriors, Helez carried this geographic identifier as part of his formal title. The term connects military prowess to local identity, showing how David's elite fighters came from across Judah's territory. This hometown designation became an honorific, permanently linking Helez's name with his place of origin.

gloss_terse: Piltai: a priestly family head during the high priesthood of Joiakim
gloss_readable: Piltai appears in Nehemiah 12:17 as the head of a priestly family during the time of the high priest Joiakim, in the generations following the return from Babylon. These lists in Nehemiah 12 trace the continuity of priestly families, demonstrating that despite the exile's disruption, the legitimate priesthood survived and was reconstituted in Jerusalem. Piltai represents one link in this chain of authorized ministry. The careful preservation of such names reflects how seriously post-exilic Judaism took questions of lineage and authorization for sacred service.

senses.1: A personal name in Nehemiah 12:17, identifying the head of a priestly family during the high priesthood of Joiakim in post-exilic Jerusalem. Piltai's inclusion in this genealogical record served to establish the continuity and legitimacy of the reconstituted priesthood after the Babylonian exile. These family lists documented which priestly lines maintained their authorization for temple service, crucial for the restored community's confidence in the validity of their worship.

gloss_terse: Pelaiah: a descendant of David in the post-exilic period
gloss_readable: Pelaiah appears in 1 Chronicles 3:24 in the genealogy of David's royal line, several generations after the exile. Though the Davidic throne no longer existed in political terms, these genealogies preserved the royal lineage, maintaining hope in God's covenant promises to David. Each name represented continuity—the line of promise hadn't died out. For post-exilic Jews, knowing who descended from David mattered both for immediate legal questions and for eschatological hope: one day, a son of David would restore the kingdom.

senses.1: A personal name in 1 Chronicles 3:24, identifying a descendant of David several generations after the Babylonian exile. Pelaiah's inclusion in the royal genealogy served to document the continuation of David's line even when no king sat on the throne. These post-exilic records maintained the connection to God's covenant with David, preserving both legal lineage and messianic hope that eventually a son of David would restore the kingdom.

gloss_terse: Decision, arbitration; the rendering of judicial judgment or mediation
gloss_readable: This term appears in Isaiah 16:3, where Moab is urged to 'give decision' or 'act as judge' for Judean refugees fleeing from oppression. The word relates to the office of an arbiter or mediator—one who weighs cases and renders fair judgment. Isaiah envisions Moab providing judicial protection, making righteous decisions on behalf of the vulnerable. The term emphasizes the active, functional aspect of justice: not just holding judicial office but actually performing the work of discernment, weighing evidence, and pronouncing fair verdicts that protect the innocent.

senses.1: Refers to the act of rendering decision or performing the office of a judge/arbiter in Isaiah 16:3, where Moab is called to exercise judicial protection for Judean refugees. The term emphasizes the functional aspect of justice—actively weighing cases, making determinations, and pronouncing verdicts that defend the vulnerable. It's not passive authority but active arbitration, the actual work of discerning right from wrong and enforcing that determination.

gloss_terse: For judges; requiring judicial attention, a crime calling for legal judgment
gloss_readable: This adjective appears in Job 31:28, where Job declares that certain sins would be 'iniquity for judges'—crimes requiring judicial attention and punishment. In his oath of innocence, Job lists secret sins that might escape human notice, then names those that would be publicly prosecutable if discovered. Idolatry falls into this latter category: not just personal betrayal of God but a crime against the community requiring legal judgment. The phrase indicates offenses that fall under earthly courts' jurisdiction, violations so serious they demand judicial intervention.

senses.1: An adjective in Job 31:28 describing iniquity that falls under judges' jurisdiction—crime requiring formal judicial action. Job uses this phrase to characterize idolatry as not merely personal sin but public crime, an offense against the covenant community that earthly courts should prosecute. The term distinguishes between private failings and violations so serious they demand legal judgment, crimes that call for the magistrate's attention and punishment.

gloss_terse: Judgment, rendering decisions; the judicial or prophetic function of determining cases
gloss_readable: This term appears in Isaiah 28:7, in Isaiah's denunciation of priests and prophets who 'stagger in judgment' because of drunkenness. The word refers to the active work of rendering decisions—whether judicial verdicts or prophetic oracles. Both priests and prophets had decision-making roles: priests taught Torah and decided ritual cases, prophets delivered God's word to guide the nation. When these leaders were drunk, their judgment—their capacity to perceive rightly and decide wisely—was compromised. The term captures the critical moment when a determination must be made, and incompetent leadership fails.

senses.1: Refers to the act of rendering judgment or making decisions in Isaiah 28:7, where drunken priests and prophets are condemned for staggering 'in judgment.' The term describes the critical function of discerning and deciding—whether judicial verdicts or prophetic declarations. Israel's spiritual leaders held this responsibility, and their intoxication didn't just embarrass them personally; it disabled them from performing their essential role as decision-makers who guided the nation.

gloss_terse: Palal: a wall-builder who helped repair Jerusalem's fortifications under Nehemiah
gloss_readable: Palal is mentioned in Nehemiah 3:25 as one of the individuals who worked on rebuilding Jerusalem's wall. The name itself relates to prayer or intercession—fitting for someone engaged in the sacred work of restoring God's city. Each builder named in Nehemiah 3 represents both literal construction and spiritual rebuilding. They weren't just stacking stones but reconstituting Jerusalem as a holy city, a physical declaration that God's people had returned and would not be moved again. Palal's particular section included repairs near the projecting tower and the king's upper house.

senses.1: A personal name in Nehemiah 3:25, identifying one of the builders who repaired Jerusalem's wall following the Babylonian exile. Palal worked on a section near the projecting tower and the king's upper palace. As with all the builders named in this chapter, Palal's work was both practical and symbolic—reconstructing physical defenses while demonstrating the returned community's determination to establish Jerusalem securely as God's city.

gloss_terse: Pelaliah: a priest, son of Amzi, in post-exilic Jerusalem
gloss_readable: Pelaliah appears in Nehemiah 11:12 as a priest serving in post-exilic Jerusalem, specifically identified as son of Amzi. The name means something like 'Yahweh has intervened' or 'Yahweh has judged'—theologically rich for a priest whose role involved mediating God's intervention through sacrifice and blessing. These priestly genealogies in Nehemiah document the legitimate restoration of temple service after the exile. Pelaliah represents one family maintaining the authorized priestly line, ensuring that worship in the restored temple was conducted by properly credentialed descendants of Aaron.

senses.1: A personal name in Nehemiah 11:12, identifying a priest serving in Jerusalem after the return from Babylon. As son of Amzi, Pelaliah was part of the reconstituted priestly establishment in the restored temple. His name, meaning something like 'Yahweh has intervened,' reflects the theological conviction that undergirded these genealogies: God had indeed intervened to restore His people and His worship, and Pelaliah's priestly service was evidence of that divine faithfulness.

gloss_terse: To a certain one; to someone unnamed or unspecified (Aramaic pronoun)
gloss_readable: This Aramaic phrase appears in Daniel 8:13, where one holy one speaks 'to a certain one'—someone unspecified. It's a deliberate vagueness, like saying 'to someone' or 'to so-and-so.' The text doesn't identify either the speaker or the addressee, maintaining an air of mystery about the angelic conversation Daniel overhears. This indefiniteness serves a literary purpose: Daniel is witnessing heavenly dialogue not meant for him initially, catching only fragments of a larger celestial discussion about the little horn's blasphemies and the sanctuary's desecration.

senses.1: An Aramaic phrase meaning 'to a certain one' or 'to someone' in Daniel 8:13, where one holy one speaks to another unnamed holy one. The deliberate vagueness serves to emphasize the mysterious nature of the angelic conversation Daniel overhears. Rather than identifying the speakers precisely, the text preserves the sense that Daniel is witnessing a fragment of heavenly discourse not originally addressed to him, heightening the revelatory nature of what he learns about the appointed time.

gloss_terse: Tremble, shudder; shake violently in response to cosmic disturbance
gloss_readable: This Hithpael verb appears in Job 9:6, describing how the earth's pillars shudder when God shakes the earth in his anger. It's violent, involuntary trembling—the kind that comes from cosmic-level disturbance. The image is of the very foundations of creation responding to divine power with convulsive shaking. Job uses this metaphor to illustrate God's overwhelming might: if even the pillars that support the world tremble at His touch, how can a human being hope to stand in legal dispute with Him? The term captures existential terror at the cosmic scale.

senses.1: A Hithpael verb describing violent shuddering in Job 9:6, specifically of the earth's pillars when God shakes the world. The term conveys involuntary, convulsive trembling in response to overwhelming force—not gentle swaying but violent shaking that threatens structural integrity. Job uses this image to emphasize divine power: even creation's foundations cannot remain stable when God manifests His anger, making human resistance unthinkable.

gloss_terse: The corners; angular points or extremities of structures or territories
gloss_readable: This plural form appears in Zechariah 14:10 describing the geographical extent of elevated Jerusalem in the eschatological vision. The 'corners' refer to angular points or extremities—the city's edge points that define its boundaries. In architectural contexts throughout Scripture, 'corners' mark critical structural points, places where walls meet and strength is concentrated. In territorial description, corners delimit the extent of land. Zechariah's use suggests completeness: from one corner to another encompasses the whole, all of Jerusalem transformed and elevated, from Benjamin Gate to the site of the former gate, to the Corner Gate.

senses.1: Refers to corners or angular points in Zechariah 14:10, defining the extent of Jerusalem in the prophet's vision of the city's future elevation. The term marks boundary points—where walls meet, where territory is delimited. By naming specific corners (from one gate to another), Zechariah encompasses the whole city, suggesting complete transformation. Corners served as reference points for describing both architectural structures and territorial extent.

gloss_terse: Pannag: an unknown food product or grain, possibly confections or special cakes
gloss_readable: This enigmatic word appears once in Ezekiel 27:17, in the list of goods Judah and Israel traded with Tyre. It's mentioned alongside wheat from Minnith, honey, oil, and balm—all food products. Ancient versions guessed at its meaning, and modern scholars remain uncertain. Some suggest it was a type of confection or specialty grain product. The Spanish preserves the Hebrew term transliterated (pannag), acknowledging the uncertainty. What's clear is that it was something valuable enough to list among Tyre's important imports, presumably something delicious or luxurious that wealthy Phoenicians desired.

senses.1: An unknown food product mentioned in Ezekiel 27:17 among the trade goods Judah and Israel supplied to Tyre. Listed with wheat, honey, oil, and balm, it was presumably edible and valuable—perhaps confections, special cakes, or a grain preparation. The uncertainty of its identification hasn't stopped translators from attempting renderings like 'confections,' though many simply transliterate the Hebrew. Whatever pannag was, it represented something desirable enough to be worth international trade.

gloss_terse: One who pampers; someone who indulges or treats with excessive leniency
gloss_readable: This Piel participle appears in Proverbs 29:21, warning that 'one who pampers his servant from youth will find him a son in the end'—though the meaning of the final word is disputed. The term describes indulging or treating with excessive softness, removing normal discipline or expectations. The proverb warns against blurring the master-servant boundary through over-indulgence. A servant raised without proper structure and expectations becomes presumptuous, expecting treatment as a son and heir rather than accepting his role. The word captures the problematic tendency to spare someone from necessary discipline, creating entitlement.

senses.1: A Piel participle in Proverbs 29:21 describing someone who pampers or indulges a servant, treating him with excessive leniency from youth. The term suggests removing appropriate boundaries and discipline, allowing improper familiarity. The proverb warns that this approach backfires: the servant grows presumptuous, perhaps even expecting inheritance rights. The verb captures the problematic side of kindness—indulgence that undermines proper structure and creates entitlement rather than gratitude.

gloss_terse: Go through, pass between; traverse or carefully examine (uncertain derivation)
gloss_readable: This imperative appears in Psalm 48:13, where worshipers are told to 'walk about Zion, go around her, number her towers, consider her ramparts, go through her palaces.' The final verb is textually uncertain—other suggestions include 'inspect' or 'consider carefully.' In context, it's part of a liturgical procession around Jerusalem, meditating on the city's defenses as evidence of God's protection. Whatever the precise nuance, it involves careful attention, possibly walking through or between structures to examine them thoroughly. The psalm invites not casual observation but deliberate contemplation of how God preserves His city.

senses.1: An imperative verb in Psalm 48:13 (textually uncertain), apparently meaning 'go through' or 'pass between,' referring to Jerusalem's palaces. Part of a liturgical call to circumambulate and carefully observe Zion's fortifications, the term suggests deliberate traversing—walking between or through structures to examine them closely. The psalm invites worshipers to meditate on the city's strength as evidence of divine protection, and this verb contributes to that call for careful, contemplative observation.

gloss_terse: In Pas-dammim: at a place name meaning 'boundary of blood' or 'portion of blood' in Judah
gloss_readable: This place name appears in 1 Chronicles 11:13, identifying where one of David's mighty men performed a famous act of valor, defending a barley field against the Philistines. The parallel account in 1 Samuel 17:1 gives a slightly different form (Ephes-dammim). The name likely means 'boundary of blood' or 'portion of blood,' perhaps commemorating a battle. Located in western Judah between Azekah and Socoh, about 16 miles southwest of Jerusalem, it was in the border region where Philistine and Israelite territories met—hence frequent conflicts and a name referencing bloodshed.

senses.1: A place name in 1 Chronicles 11:13, identifying a battle site in western Judah where one of David's elite warriors defended a field against Philistine raiders. The name, meaning approximately 'boundary of blood,' reflects the region's violent history as a contested border zone between Israelite and Philistine territories. Located near Socoh and Azekah, Pas-dammim witnessed multiple conflicts, its name preserving the memory of bloodshed in this frontier region.

gloss_terse: An abundance, a handful; plenty or sufficient amount (textually uncertain)
gloss_readable: This word appears in Psalm 72:16, in a vision of abundance during the ideal king's reign: 'an abundance of grain in the land.' The Hebrew is textually difficult—some scholars suggest reading a different word entirely (such as 'plenty' from another root). Whatever the precise term, the image is clear: grain so plentiful that even on mountaintops there's abundance. This isn't ordinary agricultural yield but miraculous, Eden-like fertility where even marginal land produces bountifully. The term captures the overflowing nature of blessing under righteous rule—not mere sufficiency but superabundance.

senses.1: A textually uncertain term in Psalm 72:16, apparently meaning 'abundance' or 'handful,' referring to grain during the messianic king's reign. The phrase envisions such agricultural bounty that even mountaintops—normally unsuitable for grain—produce abundantly. Whether the specific word means a literal handful or symbolic abundance, the context makes clear it represents extraordinary fertility, the curse of Genesis 3 reversed under righteous rule.

gloss_terse: Pasakh: an Asherite, son of Japhlet in tribal genealogy
gloss_readable: Pasakh appears in 1 Chronicles 7:33 in the genealogy of Asher, identified as one of Japhlet's sons. These tribal genealogies served multiple purposes: establishing inheritance rights, maintaining tribal identity, and preserving historical memory even when political structures changed. Though Pasakh himself plays no narrative role, his inclusion ensures that his family line remained documented among Asher's descendants. For post-exilic readers, these genealogies affirmed continuity—the tribes hadn't been lost, their family structures persisted, and Israel's identity as twelve tribes remained intact.

senses.1: A personal name in 1 Chronicles 7:33, identifying a descendant of Asher through the line of Japhlet. Pasakh represents one link in Asher's tribal genealogy, preserved in the Chronicles' comprehensive documentation of Israel's family structures. Though he performs no actions in the biblical narrative, his inclusion maintains the record of Asherite families, part of the Chronicler's project of affirming tribal continuity and legitimacy across generations.

gloss_terse: Have vanished, disappeared; ceased to exist or be found
gloss_readable: This verb appears in Psalm 12:1, in a lament that 'the faithful have vanished from among mankind.' The term describes complete disappearance—not just becoming rare but seeming to have ceased to exist. It's stronger than declining in number; it suggests dissolution, as if the category itself has been erased. The psalmist expresses existential loneliness: looking around and finding no one godly, no one trustworthy. Whether literal depopulation or hyperbolic despair, the verb captures the horror of finding oneself alone in one's commitment, the godly having apparently vanished from the earth.

senses.1: A Qal perfect verb in Psalm 12:1 describing the faithful as having vanished or disappeared from among humanity. The term conveys more than numerical decline—it suggests complete disappearance, as if the godly have been dissolved or erased from existence. The psalmist's lament uses this strong verb to express his sense of isolation: scanning his world and finding no one who shares commitment to covenant faithfulness, as if all the faithful had simply vanished.

gloss_terse: Pispah: an Asherite, son of Jether in tribal genealogy
gloss_readable: Pispah appears in 1 Chronicles 7:38 in the genealogy of Asher, listed as one of Jether's sons. Like many names in these genealogical sections, Pispah has no narrative associated with him—he exists in Scripture purely as a link in the chain of Asherite families. The Chronicler's inclusion of such names served to document the complete tribal structure, ensuring that every recognized family line was accounted for. For the post-exilic community, these comprehensive lists affirmed that Israel's tribal identity remained intact despite the disruptions of conquest and exile.

senses.1: A personal name in 1 Chronicles 7:38, identifying a descendant of Asher through Jether's line. Pispah has no individual narrative but serves as one entry in the Chronicler's systematic documentation of tribal genealogies. His inclusion helps establish the completeness of Asher's family records, part of the larger project of demonstrating continuity and legitimacy for all of Israel's tribes despite the exile and dispersion.

gloss_terse: I will groan; utter sounds of labor or distress (onomatopoetic)
gloss_readable: This verb appears in Isaiah 42:14, where God declares 'I will groan like a woman in labor.' It's an onomatopoetic word, capturing the involuntary sounds of intense effort or distress. In this remarkable passage, God uses the imagery of childbirth to describe His coming intervention—He has been silent and restrained for a long time, but now He will 'gasp and pant' as He brings forth deliverance. The groaning isn't weakness but the sound of powerful exertion, the straining necessary to birth something new. It humanizes God while emphasizing the costly, effortful nature of salvation.

senses.1: A verb in Isaiah 42:14 where God says 'I will groan like a woman in labor,' using childbirth imagery to describe His coming intervention on Israel's behalf. The onomatopoetic term captures involuntary sounds of intense effort, not weakness but powerful exertion. After long restraint, God will 'gasp and pant'—spending Himself in the work of delivering His people. The groaning expresses the costly, effortful nature of bringing forth salvation, comparing divine intervention to labor pains.

gloss_terse: Peullethai: a Levite gatekeeper, son of Obed-edom in David's time
gloss_readable: Peullethai appears in 1 Chronicles 26:5 as one of the sons of Obed-edom, blessed by God and assigned as gatekeepers for the temple. Obed-edom's family received special divine blessing after he had housed the ark of God, and his descendants continued in temple service as doorkeepers. Gatekeepers weren't merely ceremonial; they controlled access to holy space, maintained order during worship, and guarded sacred precincts. Peullethai inherited both this practical responsibility and the honor of his family's association with the ark, their role perpetuating the divine favor shown to Obed-edom.

senses.1: A personal name in 1 Chronicles 26:5, identifying one of Obed-edom's sons who served as a Levitical gatekeeper in the temple during David's organization of worship. Peullethai's family received special divine blessing related to their care for the ark, and this blessing extended into their ongoing service as doorkeepers. His role involved controlling access to the sanctuary, maintaining order, and protecting holy space—significant responsibilities that combined practical security with religious sanctity.

gloss_terse: Paarai: one of David's mighty warriors from Arabah
gloss_readable: Paarai is named in 2 Samuel 23:35 as one of the elite 'mighty men' who formed David's personal guard and distinguished themselves in combat. The parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 11:37 gives his name as Naarai, likely representing textual variation or alternate tradition. These warriors came from diverse backgrounds and regions across Israel, their roster reading like a honor roll of heroism. Paarai's identification as 'the Arbite' (from Arabah) locates him geographically, possibly from the Jordan Valley region. His inclusion among the Thirty immortalized his valor in service of David's kingdom.

senses.1: A personal name in 2 Samuel 23:35, identifying one of David's elite 'mighty men'—the warriors who formed his personal guard and distinguished themselves through extraordinary combat feats. Designated 'the Arbite,' Paarai likely came from the Arabah region. His inclusion in this select roster permanently commemorated his valor and loyalty to David. The parallel text in 1 Chronicles gives the name as Naarai, reflecting textual tradition variation.
